title: Cincinnati, the drunk comedy number, and Carl Clauve's invitation
summary: The Potter band plays Goodman's Palm Gardens in Cincinnati, where Davison does a comedy song and banjoist Carl Clauve says a recording band needs him.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: You did start doing some singing---
Oh, I always did singing. Yes.
And you started to do a little bits, comedy didn't you?

Well, about the time we went to Cincinnati - he was offered a job and we went to Cincinnati. He was offered a job in Cincinnati and this is the first time, of course, I had ever seen a big city. And, so, I did a little song at that time - it was called, "Save Your---
It was a Bert Williams (inaudible).

Yeah - "Save a Little Dram For Me." And, I used to do a drunken act on that. And, I would pretend I was drinking out of a bottle and as I did this little preaching bit, I got drunker and drunker which was my big comedy number. And, all that stuff. So, we went to Cincinnati and, uh, gosh, we were--- that summer,
That was 1923---
It was the early part of that summer - we must have went in there in April - around April---
I think so - I think it was the heart of the summer.
Yes and we were playing there
and they packed them in this place; it was a beer garden.
It was called---
No -it was called---
It's a place in Walnut Hills--
Yeah.
Palm Goodman's Gardens.

Goodman's Palm Gardens and it was a beautiful place and it had a summer garden outside with a shell in it and if it got too warm inside, we'd go out in the garden and play. And, it was one of those--- well, it's almost like the neighborhood tavern today. You know, it was mostly neighbors around there came to the place. It was packed all the time with people. And, while I was there, there was a fellow that came in one night - introduced himself as Carl Clauve and he was a banjo player and he said, "I'm with the big band here," he said. And, he said -- "Gee, we need a trumpet player in that band" and he said, "I've been listening to you all night", he said -- "You're just the kind of a trumpet player we need."
He specified that he needed a hot trumpeter---
They had two trumpets, you see.
call "hot trumpet." You were playing what people came to
Well, I suppose - if you want to---
Yes. You were taking jazz solos and that sort of thing already with Roland Potter.
Yes - you know, they'd give me a
chorus here and there. Of course, as corny as it was in those days--
And, there weren't that many hot trumpeters around - were there?

No, not really. No, not at that time. But, anyway, Carl said - gee, you're up our alley. I mean, we're looking for someone like you - would you be interested? And, when he told me that the band was a recording band, boy, I couldn't believe that.
